subtype: Approach: asking for a review after a raise is refused [Revision]
passage: The finance head had frozen raises for the year, and Yogesh said so with an apologetic face. Vaibhav had half expected the answer, and had a second question ready. "Could we write down a date to look at it again, and what you'd want to see from me by then?" That evening Yogesh emailed: review in March, and three targets, which were two client launches on time, one process document, and mentoring the new hire. Vaibhav pinned the email above his desk. Six months later he brought a one-page sheet: all three targets met, with dates. "I'd like to reopen the raise," he said. Yogesh read it and nodded. "I can take this to finance with a straight face."

qa.a: The review was scheduled for March.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel when hearing that raises were frozen?
qa.a: Vaibhav had half expected it, so he was disappointed but steady, with a second question ready.

qa.q: What else could Vaibhav do during the six months, and why?
qa.a: Vaibhav could ask Yogesh for feedback at the halfway point, because it shows whether the targets are on track before the review.

qa.q: How might Yogesh have seen Vaibhav's request for a written review date?
qa.a: Yogesh probably felt relieved that Vaibhav accepted the news constructively, and could support the raise more easily with clear targets.

grounding: Illustrates asking for a written review date and clear targets when a raise is refused, then reopening the talk six months later with results.

subtype: Approach: asking for a review after a raise is refused [Revision]
passage:
Tushar had asked for a raise in March, and Bidisha, his manager at the Kolkata insurance office, had been honest. "There's a freeze until the new financial year. I can't do it now."
He left her cabin feeling flat. Then he went back ten minutes later.
"I understand about the freeze. Could we put a review date in writing, and agree what I'd need to show by then?"
Bidisha opened her laptop. "October. If you cut claims processing time on your team and train the two new joiners, that's a strong case." She emailed him the note that afternoon.
Tushar printed it and stuck it inside his drawer.
In October, he walked in with a single page: processing time down by a clear margin, both joiners working independently, a thank-you note from the regional head.
Bidisha read it and smiled. "Okay. Let's talk properly this time."

qa.q: When was the written review date?
How did Tushar feel when he first left Bidisha's cabin?
qa.a: He felt flat and disappointed after hearing about the freeze.

qa.q: What else could Tushar have done in the months before October?
qa.a: He could have kept a monthly note of his progress on both targets and checked in with Bidisha halfway, so there were no surprises.

qa.q: How does the October meeting look from Bidisha's side?
qa.a: Bidisha has clear results against targets she set herself, so she can support a raise with confidence instead of guessing.

grounding: It shows someone who is refused a raise asking for a written review date and clear targets, then reopening the talk with results in hand.

subtype: Approach: asking for a review after a raise is refused [Revision]
passage:
"I'm sorry, Vikas. The budget's closed for this year. I can't raise your pay now."
Vikas nodded slowly. "I understand, Nitin. Can I ask something else, then?"
"Go on."
"Could we set a date to revisit this, in writing? And tell me exactly what would make the case strong."
Nitin looked surprised. "Most people just walk out upset." He thought. "Six months. Say, first week of July. If your team's bug backlog is halved and you handle the payments release, I'll take it to the committee."
"Can you email that?"
"Today."
—
"Nitin, it's July. You have a minute?"
"Sure. I remember."
Vikas put a printout on the desk. "Backlog halved in May. Payments release went live last week with no rollbacks."
Nitin read it twice. "That's exactly what we agreed. I'll take it to the committee on Friday."

qa.q: When did Nitin suggest they revisit the raise?
How might Vikas have felt hearing that the budget was closed, and how can you tell Vikas stayed steady?
qa.a: Vikas was likely disappointed but stayed calm and determined, nodding slowly and asking for a written date and targets instead of walking out upset.

qa.q: What else could Vikas try if the committee still said no in July?
qa.a: Vikas could ask what was missing and agree the next review date, or look at the market range for the role to understand the options.

qa.q: How does Vikas's approach look to Nitin?
qa.a: Nitin is surprised and seems to respect it, since clear written targets give Nitin a solid case to take to the committee.

grounding: It shows someone refused a raise asking for a written review date and targets, then reopening the talk six months later with results.
